utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Can I ask the registrar to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-12, the Prosecutor versus Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Rajic, can you understand me in a language that you can understand? The microphone works? Thank you. You may sit down. Can we have the appearances now for the sake of the record. First the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Kenneth Scott, for the Prosecution. I am joined today by Ms. Josee D'Aoust, and also our case manager, Ms. Skye Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Doris Kosta, and I am Defence counsel for Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Before we start the proceeding, I want to express the feeling of the Chamber of satisfaction that the matters that were raised at the previous hearing seems to have been resolved in a satisfactory way, and I'm very pleased to see Mr. Rajic here present at the hearing today. Let me recall the ordering to the proceedings that has been agreed upon with the parties. So we will have first the submissions of the Prosecution, which will last for 50 minutes, more or less, which then will be followed by questions by the Judges. The same applies to the Defence: We will have 50 minutes for the Defence, also followed by questions by the Judges. Then we will have a statement by Mr. Rajic, also followed by questions. And the session will be ended with closing arguments by the Prosecution and the Defence. We will have a short break after the Prosecution's submissions. I hope this is still in agreement with all of you. Let me start by first summarising what this case is about. The case concerns the attacks of 22/23 October 1993, upon the villages of Stupni Do and Bogos Hill in Vares municipality which caused the deaths of several Bosnian Muslim men, women, elderly, and children. The case also concerns the round-up of a large number of Bosnian Muslims in Vares town and their subsequent inhumane treatment in two schools; the Ivan Goran Kovacic school and the Vladimir Nazor school. As a commander of the 2nd Operational Group, based in Kiseljak, Mr. Rajic ordered these attacks and the rounding up of civilians, knowing the substantial likelihood of the criminal consequences of the orders. In October, on the 26th of October, Mr. Rajic pleaded guilty to counts 1, 3, 7, and 9 of the amended indictment, each of these counts being a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and each punishable under Article 2 of the Tribunal's Statute. His guilty plea was based on a plea agreement entered into on the 25th of October with the Prosecutor, to which the factual basis of the plea is appended. And the next day, on the 26th of October, the Trial Chamber entered a finding of guilt for those four counts. The Prosecution indicated that it would ask the remaining counts in the amended indictment to be dismissed at the sentencing hearing. I take it that this will happen in the course of today's hearing. Following the hearing of the 26th of October there has been an additional clarification decision on the convictions entered following some confusion that may have been raised by the way in which the plea agreement was formulated. So following that clarification decision, it is now very clear that the conviction that was entered was a conviction under Article 7(1) of the Statute and not under Article 7(3) of the Statute. Important in the chronology of this case is also that in July of last year the Prosecutor filed a motion before the Referral Bench to have the amended indictment referred to Bosnia and Herzegovina under Rule 11 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and Mr. Rajic opposed this referral. On 10 November of last year, which was after the guilty plea, on 10 November of last year the Prosecution informed the Referral Bench of its intention to withdraw the motion for referral upon completion of the sentencing procedure. What we are doing today in this hearing, or the purposes of today's hearing is the sentencing. So we are hearing the oral presentation of the evidence on both sides. We are not discussing the facts, so this is something that we leave behind us because of the plea agreement and the conviction that has been entered already on that basis. So may I now turn to Mr. Scott to submit the highlights of the Prosecution sentencing brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Before I proceed with our comments or our argument, I would just like to point out a couple of procedural matters. First, two of the photos that I have been referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I can't switch mine off. I should be able to switch it off. Mine's off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll begin again, Your Honour. There are two photos that will be displayed in the course of our presentation this afternoon, and to avoid any problems or confusion, I wanted to indicate that these had previously, at the Prosecution's request, been placed under seal. However, on further reflection and consideration, we do not believe that there is any need for these documents or photos to be confidential and can be shown. They are hard pictures, if you will, in terms of the emotional impact, but they do not need to be protected in terms of their confidentiality in terms of the victims at this point in time. Secondly, just so there's no misunderstanding, when I make references to some statements by witnesses who are still protected, I have paraphrased or omitted certain references to names just to protect that. So if counsel or someone might detect some discrepancy, it would be because I have paraphrased a couple of things to protect sensitive information. May it please the Court, Your Honours, for the people of Stupni Do, the 23rd of October, 1993, was hell. There is simply no other way to describe it. On that day, the village of Stupni Do became a blazing inferno of death and destruction. The sounds of gun-fire and shelling of explosions were later replaced by the sounds of women and children and, indeed, I am sure grown men crying. Unfortunately, Stupni Do was one of the signature events in the Balkan wars, together with the Sarajevo siege, Ahmici, Vukovar Hospital, Mostar, and Srebrenica. Only five days after this massacre, only five days, on the 28th of October, 1993, the atrocity came before the United Nations Security Council, which demanded an investigation. If I can have that on the screen, please. From the UN report, the Secretary-General's report, we have this excerpt: "The horrendous crimes committed by the HVO in Vares and Stupni Do in October 1993 were immediately broadcast and reported around the world and received the United Nations Security Council's immediate attention. On the 28th of October" -- again, as I've said, only five days after these horrendous events -- "the president of the Security Council requested that the Secretary-General report on the massacre as soon as possible. The Secretary-General communicated his report -- his subsequent report on the 10th of February, 1994, indicating the results of an investigation at that time by the military police of the United Nations Protection Force," or UNPROFOR, "which stated in part: "Investigations to date have shown that crimes against innocent civilians in Stupni Do took place on the 23rd of October 1993. 23 victims so far have been clearly identified. A further 13 villagers are unaccounted for and presumed dead, bringing the preliminary total number of victims to 36. The main suspects for the commission of these crimes appear to be extremist elements of the Croatian Defence Council from Kiseljak, Travnik, and Kakanj, under the command of Ivica Rajic. The HVO Bobovac Brigade, operating under its deputy commander, Kresimir Bozic, prevented UNPROFOR units from entering the village after the attack." Paragraph 13 of the Secretary-General's report: "Investigations are continuing in order to gain as much evidence as possible with a view to identifying the perpetrators for eventual trial before the International Tribunal for the Prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations ..." that is, this Tribunal. "The Security Council will be kept informed of the progress made in the investigation." And Ms. President, Your Honours, here we are some 12 years later of this report to the UN and we have Mr. Rajic standing before us -- or seated before us, convicted of these crimes. The victims have waited a very long time for justice to be done. Before discussing the facts of the case as they relate to sentencing, let me touch on a few aspects of sentencing at the ICTY. The primary principles and purposes of sentencing in international criminal justice are, first, retribution, and that simply means giving voice to public condemnation and international rejection of the charged conduct; that is, it is wholly unacceptable to the international community. The second major principle and purpose of sentencing is individual and general deterrence. Not only concerning the accused but, perhaps even more importantly, to others. To commanders and other officials and senior persons who might be tempted or may consider engaging in similar conduct in the future. The principle of deterrence requires that the penalty imposed by the Court and by Your Honours have sufficient deterrent value to ensure that those who would consider committing similar crimes will be dissuaded from doing so. In terms of sentencing factors, the Tribunal has consistently held that the gravity of the criminal conduct is the most important factor to consider in determining sentence. This, in turn, of course, involves and must reflect the particular circumstances of the case, that is, on a case-by-case basis. As Your Honour has already indicated a moment ago, Mr. Rajic stands before this Chamber convicted on four counts; wilful killing, inhumane treatment, appropriation of property, and extensive destruction, all grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions. There can be no doubt that the crimes for which Ivica Rajic has been convicted are among the most horrific crimes that one human being can commit against another. While the number of victims in this particular case may be less than the number concerning some of the other crimes that have come before this Tribunal, that fact cannot in any way detract from the terrible nature of the crimes themselves and the horrible harms suffered by these victims. Let me give a very, very brief overview of the facts of the case as they relate to sentencing and for the Chamber's consideration. The territory of Vares municipality, which included both the town of Vares and the village of Stupni Do, was included in the 18 November 1991 declaration by Mate Boban, Dario Kordic, and others that established the so-called Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. As in other claimed municipalities, the Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities took over the Vares municipal government in early July 1992. On the 23rd of October, 1993, on the accused's, Mr. Rajic's, orders, HVO forces, including members of the Apostoli special unit of HVO military police, rounded up more than 250 primarily Muslim men in Vares town. During and as part of this process, HVO soldiers entered houses and systematically abused the inhabitants, cursing them, hitting them, forcing them out of their homes, sometimes half dressed, and systematically stole their valuables and money. The rounded-up Muslim men were detained at the Ivan Goran Kovacic and the Vladimir Nazor schools until the 3rd of November 1993. During their detention, HVO soldiers entered the schools and physically abused the prisoners. The prisoners, often including family members, were forced to beat each other. Also on the same morning of the 23rd of October, 1993, on the accused's orders, the HVO forces, including the Maturice special unit, attacked the village of Stupni Do. More than 200 civilians were in the village when the HVO launched the attack which continued until late afternoon. HVO soldiers forced civilians out of their homes and hiding places, robbed them of their valuables, executed and murdered Muslim men, women, elderly, and children, and sexually assaulted Muslim women. It was, indeed, a nightmare. When one group of Muslims - a man, nine women, and three children - attempted to flee, the man was shot and killed. His half-burned body was later found at the same location where he had been shot, and two of the women and all three children were murdered in front of their home. Three young Muslim women who escaped an initial encounter with the HVO soldiers were found hiding in a small cellar and murdered. I'll come back to these young women in a few minutes. Seven members of a Muslim family were found burned in their house, including two children ages 2 and 3. There were others, but for the purposes of this short presentation, these are the ones I will mention here. The HVO massacre at Stupni Do resulted in the deaths of at least 37 Bosnian Muslim men, women, elderly, and children. The Prosecution submits that approximately six of these persons might fairly be described as combatants or as having been combatants prior to the time they were killed. The accused has made claims that one -- perhaps an issue that may come up in today's hearing, the accused has made claims that substantially more of the victims were actually combatants, claiming that approximately ten of the victims were "fighters" and six were members of the "civil defence." Let's look, Your Honours, however, at some examples of how some of these persons who the accused says were combatants were killed. Refik Likic. He was forced with another 16 persons out of a house. All of the villagers were told to give the HVO soldiers their valuables. While this was happening, HVO soldiers cut Likic's throat with a knife. When he fell to the ground, they shot and killed him at close range. Hardly a combat death. Mehmet Likic was another victim. After Refik Likic was killed, HVO soldiers ordered these two men -- excuse me, Mr. Mehmet Likic and Edin Mahmutovic [phoen]. HVO soldiers ordered these two men to lie on the ground and then executed them at close range. Ramiz Likic. He was shot several times at close range after he refused to give an HVO soldier his money. After four Muslims were murdered in front of their very eyes, 12 other Muslim villagers were forced into a shed which the HVO soldiers then set on fire, but fortunately, the 12 Muslims were able to escape, but listen to the account of one of the victims: "I approached the window and looked outside. I could hardly see anything because there was so much smoke. I just saw one soldier down in the village, running, and fire. From the higher location of the summer house, I saw the whole village in flames. Some houses were already fully burnt down. Others were burning. No house was spared. I suddenly felt that the summer house we were confined in was burning. It was coming from the roof. The summer house was shrouded in smoke. The window that I was looking through was shut and its glass panes were hot. Then the glass panes started shattering. Each of us thought we should do something to get out. Children wept. I was the first one to suggest that we should do something to get out. The only way was to escape through the door. But everyone thought that the soldiers were outside and if we came out the door, they would kill us. I went and picked up an axe. I approached the door. I wanted to break it open but hesitated. Everybody pleaded not to do it. They said we have water and we will extinguish the fire, we will find a way out. All of us were scared they would kill us if we tried to break the doors open. We nonetheless managed to break the door. I looked outside to see whether there were any soldiers there. I did not see any. I stepped outside the summer house. I had seen two corpses being thrown into the fire of someone's house and now I wanted to look for other corpses and see whether my husband's corpse had been spared the incineration or not." The HVO soldiers continued setting houses on fire and by the 24th of October, Your Honours, the HVO forces had destroyed virtually the entire village. It was a scene of utter destruction strewn with the human wreckage of Ivica Rajic's victims. If there is any further need to confirm that the Stupni Do massacre was plainly contemplated and intended and that the behaviour there was horrible in the extreme, let me mention the statements made by HVO soldiers to some of the victims. On the 22nd of October, 1993, the day before the attack, a member of the Maturice special unit told a Muslim man who had been previously detained in the area: "Tomorrow, Balija, we are going to attack your village and kill everything that is alive and moving in it." On the 3rd of November, 1993, four HVO soldiers arrived at one of the locations in Vares where the Muslim men were being detained. One of the soldiers called out to the Muslim men: "Is there any Likic here? If there is I want to show him my condolences because I slaughtered Rama Likic in Stupni Do. Then the soldier took his knife and cut one of the prisoners' left cheek, after which he licked the blood off his knife, saying: "Balija, your blood tastes sweet. Then he cut off one of the prisoners' beard and forced him to eat it. Before the evening of the 23rd of October -- excuse me, between the evening of the 23rd October and the 26th of October, Ivica Rajic and his subordinates refused several attempts by UN Protection Forces, that is UNPROFOR, to enter Stupni Do and the two schools in Vares town when they sought to investigate what had happened at these locations. While the accused has submitted that this was done because of concerns that the Muslim forces might attempt to use UNPROFOR's presence to gain some military advantage, there was simply no justification for denying access to the schools or to the surrounding of Stupni Do. And the fact that HVO forces fired -- fired upon and hit two UNPROFOR armoured personnel carriers serving as observation posts in Vares town, with one of those vehicles -- at least one of them, conspicuously marked with the Red Cross medical emblem, or for firing at the Vares UNPROFOR headquarters located approximately seven kilometres from Stupni Do and only 300 metres, in fact, from the nearby -- or the regional HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is kindly invited to slow down a bit for interpretation and the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution submits, Your Honours, that this conduct was instead a deliberate attempt to block and impede international observers from discovering the crimes in Stupni Do and Vares until they were at least partially cleaned. On the 26th of October, 1993, when UNPROFOR finally gained access to Stupni Do, they saw that some of the houses seemed to have been used as crematoria, that some of the bodies were so destroyed that they had to have been burned repeatedly to reduce them to such a condition. With all of these things in mind, Madam President, Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to show a video clip to give the Chamber a better idea of what happened in Stupni Do, and the tape is approximately 12 minutes. Are you getting it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In case there's any confusion, there's no sound. We just wanted to just not to be confused or to be distracted by any of the background noise. So it's just the visual. Might I just add that this is -- I seem to be having a lot of technical problems. Sorry. This is looking down into Vares town, or it was a moment ago, just so you can -- it was also talked about not only about the village but also Vares town, and when you were looking down into the valley, you were looking down into Vares. Well, you're now seeing a number of these clips are actual burned bodies. These are the remains, the only thing that remained of a number of bodies that were in the village. That's the video, Your Honours. Just to show a few very briefly -- a few still photos, a couple I'll come back to in a moment, but I'm just going to go through these quite quickly at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said a few moments ago that three young Muslim women were killed in a -- murdered in a small cellar, and I would like to come back to those for a moment, if we could go back to those, those first two photographs, the still photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Three Muslim women hiding in a small cellar. One of these -- there's been apparently some claim or information that at least one of these women was a "combatant." This is what a witness said about the killing of Medina Likic and the two other women. "The sounds were coming closer and increasing. Is there anybody in the basement, a male voice coming from the other side of the door. We did not respond. We kept quiet. Somebody entered the door of the basement. The same man who was calling for us in the basement and seemed to be entering inside called out for someone by the name of Kakanjac and asked him to come in the basement. "Kakanjac asked: What? And there was a reply. I have found three Balija's women. The soldiers were cursing and swearing. I think there were just two soldiers inside the basement. Then I heard a burst of gun-fire. It was just the sound of a burst of gun-fire and I did not hear any voices, neither Nevzeta nor Medina nor Hatidza. Then the voices -- I couldn't hear them. Then the voices who were inside cursing and swearing stopped. "It was again quiet inside the basement. I realised that the voices were gone. I opened my eyes. I called Nevzeta, Hatidza and Medina in a low whisper. There was no response. I called Medina's name again and I touched her hand." One of these women in this photo. "I touched her hand and she did not respond. Nevzeta, Hatidza, and Medina still sat crouching in the pit, their heads bent over, their chins touching their chest. I tried to shake the body of my Medina, but she was dead. All three of them were dead." I think without needing to look at any additional photos from what the Chamber's already seen, let me just mention what a couple of the other observers have said about these burned bodies that you've seen both in the video and in the still photographs. One of, the UN investigators said: "The third body was that of a child. I made this judgement based on the size of the pelvis. The child may have been a female aged between 13 or 15, or a male between 10 and 12, again based on the size of the pelvis. The size of the skull also appeared to be that of a child. The skull appeared to have been smashed by some means. The edges of the skull bones were fragmented, splintered and sharp. I could not smell any gasoline but I believe the body was intentionally burned based on the amount of destruction." And from a second report on another body. "Bodies were also found inside the building but on top of the roofing material. The bodies were badly burned, but I did not see burn damage and soot on the bricks surrounding the body. Since the bodies were on top of the roofing material, this indicated to me that the bodies were placed on top of the roof after the roof was destroyed or that someone had found the bodies under the roof, removed them, and placed them on top and burned them." An additional aspect, Your Honours, of what happened at Stupni Do and in the aftermath of Stupni Do and Vares, which is a further horrendous fact about what happened there was that there was an immediate and coordinated cover-up, including at the highest levels of the HVO. This included a false investigation which was only meant to appease the international community that began immediately to make demands to know what had happened. And you saw yourself that even just five days later this event, the event that you've seen on these videos, five days later was being discussed in the Security Council in New York. In fact and as part of the cover-up, UNPROFOR was kept out of the area until at least a partial clean-up could be made. As we've already seen, bodies were virtually entirely burned down to nothing. With the knowledge of senior HVO commander Milivoj Petkovic, Ivica Rajic took on the false name Viktor Andric, and Ivica Rajic was fraudulently dismissed and replaced by Viktor Andric. In fact, neither the HVO nor the Herceg-Bosna or Croatian authorities ever punished, ever disciplined a single commander or soldier, including the accused, for the crimes committed in Vares and Stupni Do. Indeed, and to the contrary, and only a few days later on the 1st of November, 1993, when these crimes were plainly known, when they were being disused in the Security Council, that UNPROFOR had already been on the site, with everyone in the world press what had happened, on the 1st of November, Ivica Rajic was promoted to the rank of colonel after these events took place and were known. On the 10th of November, 1993, in a meeting involving the President of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, in Zagreb, it was decided, because of the events in Stupni Do and the repercussions for the Republic of Croatia that Rajic should be replaced and assigned to another area and that a public statement should be issued indicating that a judicial inquiry had been initiated. And in that meeting, President Tudjman referred to all this as a political game. Of course Rajic, in fact, was not replaced except in name. A judicial inquiry was never conducted. It was all smoke and mirrors. On the 30th of December, 1993, the HVO commander Tihomir Blaskic dismissed - I say "dismissed" - Ivica Rajic from command. According to Blaskic's own order "due to a series of apparent weaknesses in command and control and an irresponsible influence on the units while carrying out combat operations." And at the same time Commander Blaskic issued another order appointing Viktor Andric to the same exact position in the command of the same exact troops, the same exact soldiers, who committed the crimes in Vares and Stupni Do, and Viktor Andric of course was none other than the accused, the same Ivica Rajic who had been just dismissed in the other order. As we've indicated on the 10th of February, 1994, the Secretary-General made his report to the Security Council expressly stating that the main suspects included Ivica Rajic. On the 23rd of August, 1995, the accused, Rajic, was indicted by the ICTY on six counts of serious violations of international law. An ICTY arrest warrant for Mr. Rajic was provided to Croatia's minister of justice on the 8th of December, 1995, more than ten years ago -- almost 11 years ago, going on 11 years ago. On the 23rd of January, 1996, the registrar requested both the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to arrange for the publication of the indictment. Ivica Rajic, knowing that he had been indicted, knowing that he was wanted by the ICTY and the international community, willfully avoided arrest for almost eight years with the active assistance of persons and organisations in the Republic of Croatia. The accused used one or more false identities and false papers, including papers issued by the Republic of Croatia giving Ivica Rajic yet another false name, this time Jakov Kovac, and by at least the 30th of June, 1994, and continuing until at least the 30th of June, 1996, Ivica Rajic was financially supported and on the payroll, on the payroll, of the Republic of Croatia Ministry of Defence and living, at least part of the time, in Croatia while he was known by the Tudjman government to be under indictment and wanted by the international community. Finally, after much pressure and with the assistance of the ICTY, finally on the 5th of April, 2003, Mr. Rajic was arrested in Croatia and ultimately brought to this Tribunal a short time later. Just to conclude on two or three factors about sentencing. In terms of aggravating factors, Your Honour, given the horrendous nature of the crimes that you've seen this afternoon and the documents and the evidence that you've had before you and the factual basis from the other material that's been provided to you, it is hardly necessary to talk about aggravating factors; however, let me mention two. One is the accused's position of authority and its abuse. Those in positions of authority may consider such positions a matter of privilege and honour, but they also bring increased responsibility because their behaviour and its effects are so often multiplied by the conduct of their subordinates to whom they set an example and to whom they issue orders and concerning whose conduct they approve or condone. Here the accused, Mr. Rajic, abused his senior position in repeatedly failing to punish prior misconduct and repeatedly sending criminal soldiers into action. Ivica Rajic, unfortunately, in some respects, was considered a hero by many of his subordinates. They looked up at him, they wanted to emulate him, they wanted to please him. He was a hero. And the fact that various known prior misconduct had not been punished sent a not-so-subtle message to his soldiers on the 22nd to the 24th of October as to what was expected of them. Consider the HVO soldier and the accused's subordinate Miroslav Anic, also known as Firga, who only a short time prior to Stupni Do to the Stupni Do atrocities mutilated Bosnian Muslims and hung their heads in the Kiseljak town square and the accused, nonetheless, ordered this same Firga a few days later into Stupni Do. Such circumstances are directly related to the crimes committed. The failure to punish, the false investigation was a direct endorsement of these and other crimes. Once again, it sent a clear message to all the accused's subordinates that no matter what crimes they were committing, even if these crimes were exposed, even if they were strongly denounced by the international community, the perpetrators would be protected and would go unpunished, thus promoting an atmosphere and a culture of impunity. Indeed, his HVO subordinates know that Rajic's identity as Viktor Andric was a complete farce. We can only sit in this courtroom today and think that they must have thought it was quite a joke on the international community that the international community had been told that Ivica Rajic had been replaced, and all of them had to know, his soldiers, his lieutenants, his officers, there he was, using the name Viktor Andric. This could only have contributed to a further lack of respect for the international monitors when their very own HVO commanders, Petkovic, Blaskic, and Rajic, directly participated in a fraud on the international community. A second aggravating factor, Your Honours, is -- in terms of victim impact is the involvement of vulnerable and young victims. In the village of Stupni Do, the injuries caused and the harm done by the accused and his soldiers have lasted long after the 23rd of October, 1993. Individuals of whole families were traumatised. Many were left without husbands, fathers, wives, mothers, and children. The accused's victims included at least five children; one aged 13, another aged 8, two who were 3 years old, and one who was 2 years old. And at least 14 women. Some women and men were executed in front of close relatives. Young women were forced into some of the houses and were sexually abused. One of the victims lost most of his family; he lost his parents, he lost his spouse, and he lost one of his children, all in one day. While many others mourn the death of their husbands, and children. As you've seen in the still photos and in the video the village itself was almost completely destroyed. Most of the villagers lost everything they had worked for all of their lives. In Vares town, down in the valley, Muslim men were rounded up and detained in two schools where they were severely beaten or forced to beat each other, often being members of the same family. Brother made to beat brother, father made to beat son. Some of the men were so badly beaten, they were suffering -- they still suffer today in terms of some of the medical certificates that we have provided to Your Honours continuing, long-term injuries. Your Honour, before I conclude, I will mention on the other hand some mitigating factors, in fairness to the accused and consistent with the plea agreement and consistent with keeping this Chamber fully informed of the facts and circumstances surrounding the underlying conduct and what is before the Court at this time. A guilty plea is -- I'm quoting from some of the other Tribunal cases. A guilty plea is always important for the purpose of establishing the truth in relation to a crime. The establishment of the truth is a fundamental step on the way to reconciliation and prevents all forms of revisionism. For the people who, even today, say that these events never happened, for the people who, today, still say Stupni Do didn't happen like this, this guilty plea and Mr. Rajic standing up and saying: Yes, these things happen and, yes, I'm responsible for it, defeats and overcomes that revisionism. No more can someone stand up and say: These things didn't happen. As one Trial Chamber noted: Guilty pleas may contribute to the process of reconciliation among the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, while the Prosecution in no way minimises -- I'm sure you can tell by my comments and what we've put before you this afternoon. While we in no way minimise the horrible crimes concerning which this accused has pled guilty and stands convicted, it must be said that this accused is the only one concerning these crimes who to date has stood up and said: I am guilty, and I accept responsible for what I did. The Prosecution submits that the accused's guilty plea is, indeed, a factor which the Chamber can and should consider in determining an appropriate sentence. One last factor is cooperation. Rule 101(B)(ii) specifically identifies: "Substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor as a mitigating factor to be considered in sentencing." The weight to be attached to cooperation: "Depends on the extent and the quality of the information provided to the Prosecution." We inform the Chamber, as we have in our papers, that Mr. Rajic has indeed substantially cooperated with the Prosecutor and he continues to do so. He has met with us on a number of occasions. He has provided documentation, and he has been of substantial assistance to the Prosecution, as I say, and his cooperation continues. Therefore, the Prosecution does inform the Chamber that this is a factor -- a mitigating factor that the Chamber can consider in connection with determining sentence. I should say, however, so that there's no confusion: In making its recommendation of a 15-year sentence, the Prosecution has taken both of these factors into account, that is, Mr. Rajic's guilty plea and his cooperation. And I can say to Your Honours that without those two factors our sentencing recommendation would have certainly been more severe than that. Your Honour, I have a few additional comments, but I will save them until the final comments that you have allowed on the schedule. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. I have a number of questions that I would want to ask you, six in number. The first question relates to what you consider as a factor concerning the overall gravity of the offence. If I understand you correctly, you seem to suggest that the exposure of the crimes in the Security Council and in the General Assembly is something that contributes to the gravity of the offence because it sort of offers evidence of the indignation of the international community. But I have a question about this, because would you then suggest that if there would not have been such exposure that the gravity would be less and would crimes that have not been exposed, if it -- let me call it the CNN factor, would those crimes then be less serious than crimes that have been exposed. My first question. May I list them in a row?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Okay. My second question has to do with what you were mentioned I think as an aggravating factor; mainly the fact that Mr. Rajic has not engaged in the punishment of people previous to the attacks of Stupni Do and then included a certain person, I note here Miroslav Anic as an example. My question is the following: Wouldn't that be rather a relevant element in assessing responsibility under Article 7(3) but given the fact that the conviction that has been entered is based on 7(1). Is this something that this Court can take into account as an aggravating factor still, given the fact that the Appeals Chamber in Nikolic has just reminded us of the fact that we cannot double-count elements on the one hand to assess the gravity and, on the other hand, in addition to that, to aggravate the sentence. My third question has to do with the two new aggravating circumstances that you advance, the participation in a cover-up and the absconding and obstruction -- obstructing of criminal justice. This is, as far as I can see, something that has never been decided by this Court. And I would wish to know whether what you in your additional brief give as examples of legislations where this really is taken into account as an aggravating factor, whether that is sufficient for this Trial Chamber to find a general principle of law in which we could -- on which we would base an eventual finding of an aggravating factor. My fourth question is something that does not relate to what you have said or what is in your briefs, your written briefs, but I would wish to know - and we may go into closed session if you so wish - whether there is a link with the 11 bis proceeding and whether the fact that you have withdrawn your 11 bis application waiting for the outcome of the sentencing procedure has something to do with the plea agreement. I'll drop my fifth question because otherwise I will be too long. My sixth question, and also for that we may want to go in closed session if you so decide or if you so ask us to do is: Could we get more information about what the cooperation with the Prosecution consists of and whether -- what this could possibly mean for he future in concrete cases. Thank you very much. Sorry for inundating you with such a long list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to answer as many of those as I can in open session and, indeed, it may be that as we get toward the end of your questions we might want to go into private session. In terms of the fact that these crimes were known, for instance, to the Security Council as early as 1993 and to the UN, I'm not sure that it's an aggravating factor in a -- in a technical sentencing sense, but the cover-up -- and this really relates to the issue of the cover-up as well, if I can perhaps answer both those questions at once. It goes to the accused's state of mind, his knowledge that something indeed very terrible had happened there. This was known right away, and the efforts to engage in a cover-up took place right away. And I think that that -- we submit, Your Honours, that that is evidence of state of mind. It's a -- where I come from of a guilty mind. One does not have to cover up something that is innocent, something that is not improper. And the fact that this was reported to the Security Council and in the international media put a spotlight on these events at every level, whether in Stupni Do, in Vares, in Kiseljak where Mr. Rajic was, or in Zagreb with President Tudjman, or anywhere in between. And under that spotlight, nonetheless, these very serious and very coordinated steps to cover this up, for everything from burning the bodies virtually beyond recognition, to taking on a false name, Viktor Andric, to a false investigation that Mr. Rajic now admits was intended to mislead, these things are aggravating in that broader sense. These were not -- these were not just combat deaths. These weren't -- this wasn't collateral damage. These were people that were executed followed by a cover-up. And it's in that context that we believe that the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt you for a moment. Would you to assess the state of mind of an accused also take into account what happened after the crime? To assess the state of mind when the accused committed the crime? Is that the way you look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would consider it, if you will, Your Honour, a continuing state of mind. Again, where I come from -- I was a prosecutor in the United States which perhaps you figured out by now. Where I come from a cover-up in a sense is a continuation of the crime, and it's a continuation of that sense of guilty mind. It's a continuation, another phase, a second or third, fourth phase of the crime. So we would consider it just as part of the continuing conduct that Mr. Rajic and others around him engaged in which seems to us, and we would respectfully submit this would be contrary to this being again collateral damage or two armies fighting each other in some sort of legitimate combat way. There would be no need for him to cover-up. There would be no need for a false investigation. There would be no need to take on a false name, and those are the factors that we would put before the Court for its consideration. On your second question, Madam President, on the failure to punish. Clearly in a more tradition sense I think it is directly related to 7(3), but again what we have tried to do, and again in sentencing practices that I'm accustomed to the sentencing court wants to have as much information as possible, about the individual, about the history of the individual, about what happened, the crimes that were committed, about the accused's role in those crimes, so we have simply taken the position to try to advise the Chamber of as much relevant information as possible. Perhaps if putting the word in some -- in a technical jurisprudential sense, putting the word "aggravating" on it, if that causes some concern, I think let's just look at it as it's relevant information. We would submit it's relevant information of the totality of the circumstances for the Chamber to consider. There -- having said that, the ICTY jurisprudence does recognise a direct relationship between 7(1) and 7(3), and indeed where -- the repeated failures to punish under 7(3) can become 7(1), instigation; 7(1), encouragement, approval, whatever. If you have troops -- you have subordinates with you and you repeatedly fail to punish similar conduct, after a while that sends the affirmative message that I approve, I condone, this is the conduct that I expect. And it becomes instigation, it becomes 7(1), I think at least offhand I can remember in the Blaskic trial judgement I know Judge Jorda addressed that question and made that point. Absconding. Again, Your Honour, it's the totality of the circumstances. The fact that, just as we've seen with many people at the Tribunal, whether it's Ratko Mladic or Karadzic or Gotovina or Mr. Rajic or others, it is -- great efforts have been made to avoid coming before this Tribunal. Great efforts have been made to avoid justice, and again I guess our bottom-line position on that is we think it's fair for the Chamber to be aware of that. Mr. Rajic had many opportunities to come forward. This indictment was known to him. It was published in the local -- in the regional media. He was employed by the government of Croatia at the time that arrest warrants had been given to that government. Mr. Rajic had numerous opportunities over an eight-year period to come forward and let justice be done. Either attempt to clear his name or let the process run its course, but he had many opportunities to come before this Tribunal. And it took eight years. And not then -- even not still then a surrender. He was arrested finally after eight years to come before this Tribunal. Your Honours, in terms of the 11 bis proceeding, perhaps I can give a general answer without going into private session. And then if the Chamber wants more detail, I suppose we could go into private session. There is no -- there is no link per se between the 11 bis proceeding and the guilty plea. If you will, I hope it won't be difficult to understand, those two things were simply happening on parallel tracks. There was consideration at the time that, as you know, there was - how shall I say it? - there was significant external concern about the docket of the Tribunal and the case-load of the Tribunal and referring some of these cases to the national courts. Mr. Rajic's case was identified as one which might, although having been fully proper to bring it here, I think the crimes speak for itself. Mr. Rajic was a senior HVO officer. Nonetheless, the case was identified as a candidate for the 11 bis proceeding. While all of that was happening, conversations had already taken place and been initiated about the possibility of a guilty plea, which then initially, by the fact that we're standing here this afternoon, did come about. But there was no linkage between the two. If this happens this happens, or if this, it was simply going down two parallel tracks, and once the guilty plea agreement was reached, then there was of course no reason to -- in our view to proceed under 11 bis. As to Your Honour's last question about cooperation, I think it would be better to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: We'll go in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We may have to go into private session once again because I'm going to revisit that area that our President, Judge Van den Wyngaert has just gone into. So may I ask the President if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now to deal with an aggravating factor, and the question of the avoidance of responsibility, and the escape from justice and from submission to the Court for eight years, I believe, for a number of years, I would like to make this inquiry: Do you have any evidence of when the fact of indictment first came to the attention of the accused? When did it first come to his knowledge that he was so indicted and, further, when did it come to his knowledge that a warrant had been issued for his arrest? Please give us that information, if you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The most concrete information on that point -- and by point of reference, on the 23rd of August, 1995, Mr. Rajic was indicted on the original indictment, the 23rd of August. We do know that at least by 19th of January, 1996, Mr. Rajic signed a power of attorney at a time when he happened to be in Kiseljak in Bosnia, not in Croatia but back in Bosnia, and he signed a power of attorney authorising an attorney to represent him in -- concerning the indictment against him and then seemed to disappear again. So there is a signed document. I'll have to say I don't have it in my hand this afternoon, Your Honour, but there is a signed document dated approximately the 19th of January, 1996, in which Mr. Rajic would indicate his knowledge of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm most grateful to you. There is something else, and it concerns, I believe, one of the still photos. I would like to visit that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It was, I believe, photograph number 0332706 before the one of the three Muslim ladies who had been killed, huddled together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: They were Nevzeta, Medina, and Hatidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry about my pronunciation. But in that prior photograph, the still that was shown, what was that still of? I would like to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. We're having -- I apologise to Your Honour. We're having some difficulty identifying the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY

And if you look forward the lower centre part of the photo, you see the same three women in the small little pit below -- excuse me, behind the two barrels of what looks to be potatoes or -- I would say potatoes. And the next photo is simply -- hard to say simply in this context, but is a closer photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful to you, because in that first one behind the green pail I had not initially picked up the three bodies that were there. So I'm most grateful to you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And this would be my last question, really for my own education and for clarification. I don't know if other members of the Chamber are having a difficulty with understanding. utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY

So if that could be corrected. Thank you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
