utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one additional question. In transcript page 11, lines 7 to 9, this is what you cited. You said: "On the 22nd of October, 1993, the day before the attack a member of the Maturice special unit told a Muslim man who had been previously detained in the area: "Tomorrow, Balija," and then there is something missing, "we are going to attack your village and kill everything that is alive and moving in it." Can you please complete this and explain me what that means in this special area, Balija and something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The -- yes, Your Honour. The missing word in terms of the transcript, I think that's just, with all respect, I think just a transcription error. There is no separate word, but let me just go back to my original notes because I did try to quote it directly. It was simply -- yes, it's: "Tomorrow, Balija, we are going to attack your village." So I don't think there's anything missing there. It may have been my pronunciation of the word "Balija" which may have come across sounding as if perhaps I was saying two words. If it was my mistake, I apologise for that. Balija is a very difficult -- in my experience, and having been here for some years, a very difficult term to describe except to say that it is considered to be an extremely derogatory term toward Muslims. I literally do not know a literal translation, Your Honour. And I've asked Muslims this, and I've asked people in Bosnia and people who have come to The Hague. One might -- it's almost probably too not derogatory enough to say something like you swine or you that are less than dirt, but it is an extremely derogatory term that's applied towards Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, we've been very well on schedule for this first session. We will have our break now for 20 minutes and we will resume at 10 to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: We will now hear the submissions for the Defence. Ms. Kosta.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned colleagues, after the Prosecution I shall be presenting the case in light of the mitigating circumstances and of course all the aggravating circumstances that were raised by the Prosecution. I have to say first and foremost that I agree with a comment made a moment ago by one of the members of the Trial Chamber, that we must take into consideration that the subject of -- under discussion here -- one of the points is that my client has pleaded accused -- pleaded guilty of 1, 3, 7, and 9 counts, and under 2(A) 2(B), and 2(D). Now, as far as his responsibility is concerned and accountability it has recorded under Article 7(3) of the Tribunal which states that no commander will be rid of responsibility if a crime is committed by one of his subordinates if he knew or had reason to know that the crime would be committed. I would just like to draw your attention in this portion to Article 7(4) of the Statute, and I'll explain why later on, and that is the fact that an accused person acted pursuant to an order may not be considered in mitigation of a punishment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you, Mrs. Kosta. Referring to the clarification judgement, we are very clear on the point that the guilty plea was entered for Article 7(1) and not for 7(3). So I hope we agree on that because I wasn't quite sure of what you were saying just now. But we agree that the conviction has been entered on the basis of 7(1), not 7(3). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 7(1). First of all, I'd like to say that everything that happened and the consequences of what happened in Stupni Do happened within the frameworks of war and the storms of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that the Stupni Do case was an -- was not an individual one, that is to say, it wasn't an individual location of war operations. At the -- it was taking place at the same time when the Bosnia and Herzegovinian army as well as the Serb army was active on that territory and also the very fact that an action took place in Stupni Do indicates the fact that only one day before the Stupni Do action we saw the fall of the village of Kopljari, which was a Croatian village, and also in June 1993 from the town of Kakanj itself, through an action launched by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina 13.000 Croats were expelled, and all those 13.000 Croats came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Ms. Kosta, please go a bit slower for me because I'm having a bit of difficulty keeping up and I would like to be able to comprehend. Just a little bit slower. I'm so sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, 13.000 Croats were expelled from Kakanj and they all found themselves in Vares, which means that Ivica Rajic did not go to Vares because he wanted to do so but because the entire situation with respect to the war operations demanded that intervention take place on the territory of the town of Vares. And my client did not go to Vares because he wanted to do so but on the basis of an order and after an appeal had been launched for assistance from the people of Vares. So he went there and he went several -- there with the Maturice and Apostoli units several days after those units had suffered certain casualties, namely, seven persons were killed. And I should also like to say that within the frameworks of this case and these proceedings we heard one of the commanders, Maturica. And I'd like to draw your attention here to the fact that it -- when we say "special purpose units" that is a very strong term, whereas we're talking about special purpose units then we refer to them as the Maturices and the Apostoli, Apostoles. In the legal context, military context we should draw attention to the fact that these were in fact units which at all times were placed at the disposal of the commander. If the commander deemed necessary to send them to an area where intervention was necessary, for example, where there was a breakthrough, where the separation line could not be held and so on and so forth. So there were no other attributes to these special purpose units except for the kind that I have described. That was their role. As I said, one commander was examined, and we see that we mention his name in the plea agreement and in the indictment itself. It was Como Ilijasevic, and he said when he was examined by the Prosecution, Ms. Josee was the Prosecutor, that they went but did not know why they were going specifically and that they were beside themselves because of the previous acts that had taken place and they didn't have any special weapons. I'm saying this for the following reason. Ivica Rajic, together with those units of some 200 soldiers, pursuant to orders from General Petkovic did not know what he would come across, what was waiting for him when he arrived in Vares itself. With his arrival in Vares, and when he arrived in -- before he arrived in Vares, there were written traces asking for aid and assistance with respect to the fall of the village of Kopljari. So when he reached Vares, Ivica Rajic was informed by those who were engaged in putting up Vares's defence what the situation in and in conformity with that that they were having quite a lot of problems if Bogos hill were to fall or, rather, if Stupni Do were to fall. Sizing up everything that he was told, all the information he was given, Ivica Rajic took the decision that he should take control of Bogos hill. And you can see that Bogos hill was not the subject of the indictment because it is considered to be a very important strategic military point. And at the same time they considered that if the Bogos hill were to fall, then the inhabitants of Stupni Do would leave Stupni Do and that there would be no need for any major interventions. However, when Bogos hill fell, this did not happen. The people did not leave. Neither did the soldiers who were in Stupni Do leave. And this led to additional intervention, although there is proof and evidence, and I should like to refer to that, that the inhabitants , and there were about 40 of them, we have already discussed this matter, and it -- we have reached agreement, that is to say, the Prosecution and Defence reached agreement on that fact. There are about 36 military-able men, or soldiers, as we call them, and they were individuals, and we have documents to that effect, who had packet communication and a certain amount of weapons, too. And in a military sense they were well-armed as we would term it. Now, the Prosecution, during our negotiations and discussions over the plea agreement, and also today, did not refer to and did not present to the Trial Chamber a very vital document as far as the Defence is concerned. I think it is very important to establish the legal groundworks for aggravating and mitigating circumstances for sentencing and judgement. They did not say how far the Bogos hill and Stupni Do was very vital for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So when we take a closer look at what the analysis contains, and the analysis was presented as an exhibit when we spoke about vital facts in weighing up the sentencing, then you will see that in June Ivica Rajic called upon the inhabitants of Stupni Do and Dastanski village, which are both inhabited by Muslims, to lay down their arms which the inhabitants of Dastanski did. However, the inhabitants of Stupni Do did not lay down their arms and were prevented from doing so by the BiH army and said that if NATO insisted -- if the Croatian army insisted that the town of Vares would be shelled. I am very pleased that we were able to see a moment ago photographic documents and also a film, a video was shown on the basis of which you were able to see what I'm saying, that Bogos hill and Stupni Do were very important to the BH army with respect to the town of Vares. I would like now to deal with some of the facts the Defence referred to -- or rather, the Prosecution referred to facts that are linked to show what crimes had taken place in Stupni Do and also they indicated a certain -- certain statements from interviews conducted with soldiers and people who were in Stupni Do themselves. That's what I would like to do. And may we go into private session for that because the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber took note of the fact that this was confidential information and confidential statements. So might we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to turn to this issue now dealing with the people under the command of Ivica Rajic, the troops that were under his command. We have to point out that this was a time of war. Ivica Rajic was not the one who founded either Maturice or Apostoli. They were founded by Mr. Tihomir Blaskic. And Ivica Rajic inherited them from him and he changed the name, Lucic. These were professional soldiers, soldiers concerning whom there was information that they had committed certain crimes, as the Prosecution indicated. It says that one of them cut off people's ears, one of them chopped several heads off. However, Ivica Rajic was not the person who prevented any proceedings from being instituted against these people in order to establish the criminal responsibility. The OTP is aware, the Trial Chamber is aware, because there is evidence proving this, that Ivica Rajic and the operations area at the time were the only ones in the entire HVO who did prosecute people for crimes that were committed. So in all cases when Ivica Rajic was aware of the crimes, he did bring charges against the perpetrators. These two facts pointed out by the Prosecution were not a result of Ivica Rajic's decision. No. It was a result of a decision taken by a group, and Ivica Rajic was just a member of that group, one of the members. When Maturice and Apostoli were issued an order to move towards Stupni Do and Vares, we have to say that Ivica Rajic did issue an order in legal terms. However, he, under no circumstances, ordered his people to exceed their authority which resulted in these grave consequences. Similarly, I would also like to say something about the crimes committed in Stupni Do. Now that we are discussing war crimes and conduct associated with war crimes, we have to say that there is nothing that can improve the impression of war crimes. Every war crime is an awful crime. In addition to that, we must not neglect the fact, and I'm very happy that the President of the Trial Chamber put this question to the Prosecution when she said: Do you believe that in view of the high media profile given to Stupni Do, do you think that it is in that light that the Prosecution views the gravity of the crimes committed, to which the Prosecution said: Absolutely no. However, I would like to say this, that after the crimes in Stupni Do, in a place called Donja Grabovica a massacre was committed. Croatian residents were killed. This is a well-known fact. Muslims killed 19 persons, mostly women, elderly, and children. They did not simply kill them. They slit their throats, following which they cut off each head and impaled it. I have been following all crimes which took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I have to say that this crime was never publicised by the media, at least not to the effect that, for example, a crime in Skabrnja was. I have to say that precisely because of the way that Stupni Do was presented to the public, certain arguments were brought forward to mark this or to describe this as one of the gravest crimes ever committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Let me say something about the number of the victims in Stupni Do. In the plea agreement, we agreed to the number of 36 victims. When we spoke about the sentence, however, I considered it necessary to provide to the Chamber two documents pertaining to the victims of Stupni Do. One document was drafted immediately after the events, which is exactly when the film and photographs you were shown today were made. And then the other one was made up by a commission comprising people from Stupni Do. Nowhere did they state that the fate of some other persons was not clear. On the 23rd of October, 1993, however, they apparently identified and buried the following persons, and then they go on to list the person of the last name, year of birth, and place of residence. They go on to list 17 persons. One year after that another list was drawn up which was a list of victims containing at this time 38 names. This is all I have to say about the number. In this second list you can see that the majority of the victims were marked as soldiers, and you can also see that they did not reside in Stupni Do. Let me also say that once we signed the plea agreement and once my client pleaded guilty, we acknowledged everything that took place in Stupni Do. There were, however, testimonies given by eye-witnesses, UNPROFOR representatives, monitors, and so on saying that bodies had been set on fire but did not smell of petrol. It was also said that these were the bones of bodies set on fire; however, it hasn't been possible until today to discern whether these were human bones or animal bones. We must say that this was a hand-to-hand battle. The battle was fought house to house. There was a very strong resistance put up in Stupni Do. This is under which circumstances the battle took place. We also have some witnesses saying that in one of the houses there was a barrel of oil, and as a result of all the ammunition fired this led to an explosion. Then there was also some collateral damage where people were killed by stray bullets. It would be hard to say in certain circumstances whether an injury on somebody's neck was a result of slitting throats or whether that was inflicted by a bullet which went through somebody's neck. Why are we bringing this up? We are bringing this up to show you that these are facts available in this case which must not be neglected because you have to hear the other side as well. You must hear not only about the crimes but you must also hear how the crimes came to be committed. Some things remain unclear or not clarified to this very day. In addition to this, I must point out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: May I interrupt counsel just for a second because I'm looking at the time and -- something is wrong? Maybe it's my microphone. With the time limit that is left here, we have quarter to, and we must be aware of the fact that we are bound by the plea agreement. So there are a number of things that are, unfortunately for you, not relevant anymore, and I would suggest that in the time that is left that you concentrate on the sentencing and on the gravity of the crime and the mitigating and aggravating circumstances. Sorry for interrupting you, but I think in view of the time this is an important point to make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to say something about my defence. My defence was conceived in a completely different manner until I heard your four questions, Mrs. President. I have to say that this prompted me to say something that I wasn't initially going to say. I believe this to be very important for mitigating circumstances. Now, since I have only 15 minutes left, allow me now to turn to the following circumstances. I will be very brief and clear. Ivica Rajic did not go to Vares because he wanted to. Ivica Rajic went to Vares because he was issued an order by his superior, the general who was there, which was Mr. Petkovic. Ivica Rajic was sent there in order to assess the situation and take certain action. Ivica Rajic certainly did not wish for the consequences that he is charged with to happen. He, following this, went back to Kiseljak, wrote a report. And I must say that this report was drafted on the basis of his initial knowledge, which he acquired upon entering the village of Stupni Do. He was able to see that a disproportionate force was used in the village. And based on that, in his report, he wrote sufficient -- he put in sufficient information that should have prompted his superiors to start an investigation. When Ivica Rajic reached Kiseljak -- in view of the fact that I'd like to present now -- (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: (redacted) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivica Rajic, after that, received a promotion from Tihomir Blaskic on the 1st of November, 1993. The HVO promoted him to the rank of brigadier in active service. Throughout that time you must know that the top Croatian leadership had all the knowledge about the event. And although we did not present this through our evidence, we would like to use our transcripts, which the Prosecution has as well, and that is that at a meeting with President Tudjman, the then-foreign affairs minister literally stated the following. He said that for the public that it was sufficient not only to replace him but to say that an investigation should be underway. I state that in the context of what the Prosecution said when it said that Ivica Rajic wanted to cover up the whole situation, that he himself wished to cover it up, and that that is why he changed his name later on. None of those two facts hold water. He did not cover this up, and he did not change his name because he wanted to do so. He was ordered to do so. I think we provided all the necessary documents to bear that out and showed them to the Prosecution. I think those are the mitigating circumstances. Ivica Rajic came to Croatia pursuant to orders from the Croatian authorities, and he was there in 1994 until the middle of 1996. It is true what my learned friend of the Prosecution said today, Mr. Scott, when he said yes in answer to one of your questions. When was the date that he first knew that the indictment was raised against him, and he said that it was sometime around the 9th of January, 1996. You know what happened then? He signed a power of attorney to attorney Hodak. And after talking to his attorney Hodak, who informed him of the facts, that is to say, how he should prevent his defence in order to protect Croatia and not to protect himself and not to state what actually happened, that is to say, not to tell the truth. After that Ivica Rajic revoked his power of attorney to attorney Hodak, and I must say that he was in hiding and managed to amass and collect documentation which he has now placed at the disposal of the OTP. That is what I wanted to say with respect to the aggravating circumstances. Now, the fact that he was a fugitive, let me say that his escape and the consequences of his escape have been hardest on Ivica Rajic. You might ask yourselves why. Well, because he -- the fact that he did not come before The Hague Tribunal, he did that following orders from his superiors. And during that time there were proceedings held before this Tribunal which were very bloody proceedings compared to the proceedings against General Tihomir Blaskic. With his lack of appearance, he was not able to challenge many of the assertions made by that accused, the accused who was later convicted of crimes. So that is what I want to say with regard to the aggravating circumstances that were mentioned. Now, as regards to mitigating circumstances, I would like to say the following. Ivica Rajic agreed to cooperate with The Hague Tribunal and The Hague Tribunal's Prosecution and therefore acknowledged his guilt because the reason was that he wanted in a direct way, without exposing victims to additional torture, to tell the Tribunal what actually happened in Central Bosnia or, rather, within the frameworks of his operative zone. And I would also like to stress one additional fact. Ivica Rajic, after having changed his name, because this was something that he was ordered to do, to become Viktor Andric, remained a commander of the forward command post, and I must say that at that time he took part in breaking through the corridor towards Busovaca with those same people. No -- not a single crime was ever committed in doing so. That would be all. I do apologise, but there was another circumstance that I would like to raise and that is the circumstance relating to the impossibility of UNPROFOR and UNPROFOR's entrance into Stupni Do and Vares. I would like to say that there, too, Ivica Rajic was acting upon orders from Mr. Blaskic, and they have been attached to these files. It was not an action or operation that was characteristic of Ivica Rajic. That is something that the other side did as well, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did that kind of thing, too. And we will see in the document 01813328 that it is unchallenged that Rasim Delic also prevented UNPROFOR from entering the Croatian villages and the territory where action -- the arm -- Bosnia-Herzegovina undertook its actions and operations. Ivica Rajic, and that is something that the Prosecution are aware of -- well, the question is: Why did UNPROFOR not enter Stupni Do? Well, precisely because there was a package link, and in Stupni Do you did not only have unprotected citizens, unprotected inhabitants, but it was established -- but with the entrance of UNPROFOR that this would enable soldiers who were there, who were in Stupni Do themselves, to leave. We see this on the basis of a document that was verified by the Tribunal, and the number of that document is 00793182, in which specifically one of the participants in the action on the part of the BH army in Stupni Do states the following: "We were told through packet link that us soldiers would be transported -- we soldiers would be transported by UNPROFOR, three of us with weapons, but we have to leave our weapons in the woods and also take down all our military insignia." And he says: "I took my insignia off my uniform and put on civilian clothes." So what Mr. Rajic says is this: He says that when war operations were ongoing, there was -- it was not his own will not to allow UNPROFOR to enter. There were realistic circumstances who -- which indicated the fact that UNPROFOR could be abused if it were to do so. The Defence and Mr. Rajic signed the plea agreement, the guilty plea. We stated that we were guilty of the counts in the indictment, charges made in the indictment. We have shown sincere remorse, and that is why we propose that this Trial Chamber set a sentence of 12 years for my defendant. I should also like to mention that in my written submissions I include a series of facts and figures which I consider give the Trial Chamber an overall view of the situation and that they will be able to weigh up the sentence with all these facts before it. I think that a 12-year sentence would serve as a deterrent and serve justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Can you please switch out your microphone. Thank you, counsel. I have one general observation and perhaps one question. My general observation is that in your submission now you have made a number of points that are in contradiction with the facts as they have been agreed in the plea agreement. So you must be aware of the fact that we, as the Trial Chamber, are bound by these facts and that we can't re-open a discussion on a number of items that you now want to bring under our attention or facts that you would wish to put in a different light. This is something that cannot be done at this stage in time, so I'm not going to go into that. I just want you to be aware of this. I have a question, but perhaps this is something that I can -- a question that I can address to the -- to Mr. Rajic when he makes his statement later on. The Trial Chamber knows very little about the personal circumstances of Mr. Rajic. So you have referred just now at the end to what you have been saying in your brief, but is there anything that you could ask -- could add to help the Court in assessing the personal circumstances of your client? Maybe you can leave it to him. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as to the personal circumstances of Mr. Rajic, the accused, I should like to say that the accused to the present day, to the time he appeared before the Trial Chamber, was never convicted of any crimes and he never came into coalition with the war. He was an honourable and respectable man in his unit and a member of the community in which he lived. He was also a man who, during his youth, was an honourable person. He came from a very poor background, and everything that he created he created through his own efforts and labour. He is the father of three children and is expecting a fourth child, a fourth child is on the way. His wife also works, and he was always a respected member of the community. That is what I can tell you about him. As to his other personal circumstances, I'm sure he'll be able to tell you those himself better than I would be able to. But that is what I know so far about him as a man and a member of the community. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Kosta. Judge Nosworthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Kosta, or Ms. Kosta, I had really noticed the same thing as the Presiding Judge, that you had overlooked the question and the issue of the personal circumstances of the accused. And you mentioned the fact that he was from a poor background. Do you have any other instructions or material that would help the Trial Chamber in terms of how he was brought up or the circumstances of his poor background, how he related to his parents and so on. That would go to the personal circumstances? Anything more to assist the Trial Chamber from you, his counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as his personal circumstances are concerned, I think they are facts that hold true for every normal person. That is why I didn't consider it necessary to bring any documents with me to indicate this to you. Perhaps that is a mistake on my part which I hope will not be reflected on my client. He was a very good student. He was a very good pupil during secondary school. He completed military school, and his family was a very poor one. He was supposed to be a priest. He was not linked to any ground forces. He was an engineer, a radar engineer. Unfortunately the war broke out and everything that happened happened. I would just like to add amongst the mitigating circumstances one more thing which we omitted to talk about, and that is that when we as the Defence wanted to verify the statements and testimony of certain individuals, statements given, such as Nenad Rajic, who lived in Kiseljak and who spoke about his relationship towards Muslims, in June the village of Rotilj, which is near Kiseljak, and this is in 1993, it had an exclusively Muslim population. In that village there were 1.500 Muslims who were expelled. Now, that witness, Nenad Rajic, said that Ivica Rajic paid daily visits and asked that those people -- that not a hair on the head of these people should be harmed, regardless of whether those people were supposed to be exchange or not. There was also another testimony by a witness called Jakov Bienfeld who, without any separate invitation, and there was a newspaper article written about that, came and said that Ivica Rajic during the siege of Jews in Sarajevo in 1993 organised -- that the departure of 2.000 Jews from Sarajevo without any remuneration or any conditions or strings attached. He managed to arrange for 2.000 Jews to leave Sarajevo. Those are additional data and circumstances that I could -- that I was able to give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I want to thank you, Madam Defence counsel. There was no indictment on your competence as counsel, just in an effort to get additional circumstances that might better help the Bench and the Trial Chamber in determination of its functions and issues before them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I have no special questions. Maybe the one point you underlined: "We have shown sincere remorse." Can you maybe describe us -- before we come to talk the accused himself, in how far this remorse was -- had been articulated so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the remorse was expressed in a way which might sound absurd to you, but it was done right at the outset when Mr. Rajic just found out that there was an indictment against him, that this court issued an indictment against him. And at that time he was willing to come to the court and say how things happened. Why is it that the investigation was not carried out? Why is it that things happened the way they did? Once he received the instructions that he was supposed to keep silent, that he was supposed to say that Croatia had never waged a war in the territory of Bosnia and Croatia, those were his instructions. This may sound absurd to you, but under those circumstances he started collecting documents, the documents which he disclosed to the OTP recently, and made himself available to the Prosecution as a witness in future cases. I also have to say to you that after his arrest - and this is something that can be corroborated by Mr. Scott - I was not Mr. Rajic's lead counsel at the beginning. I was just his co-counsel. But I think that back in 2003 Mr. Rajic asked or told his then-counsel, Mr. Olujic, that he was present to -- he was available to testify in the Blaskic appeal case to challenge all the untruths that were said in those proceedings. When I asked Mr. Scott whether he was aware of that, because Mr. Olujic used to claim that he had informed Mr. Scott, but Mr. Scott failed to take any action in response to this. This left me speechless. So the remorse was that and the remorse was expressed in such a way that from the first day of his arrival here my client never wanted to avoid his responsibility. And it's not that he wanted to cooperate only because of the threat posed by 11 bis proceedings, no. He expressed a desire to cooperate from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I take it, counsel, that you have no further evidence of what you are just saying than your own statement of today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no, I have no additional material to offer you. But now that we are discussing all of these mitigating and aggravating circumstances, allow me to offer another mitigating circumstance; namely, in the documentation disclosed to us and to you by the OTP, it seems clear that Stupni Do had about 50 houses and 250 inhabitants and that 50 houses had been destroyed. This has been proven. However, on page 00332872A there is a paragraph showing that the cemetery, the cemetery existing in the village of Stupni Do, was left intact, was completely preserved. In addition to that through our exhibits, we disclosed to you photographs showing that the Muslim mosque was also left intact. Why am I bringing this up? I am bringing this up to show you just what kind of an operation was conducted there in Bogos and Stupni Do, what kind of an attack it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kosta. We will now turn to Mr. Rajic. Mr. Rajic, you have the opportunity to make a statement now, and we understand that this is going to be a statement about your own feelings, looking back at what happened in October 1993 and your own involvement there. So in that case, I will refrain from asking you to make a solemn declaration. Is it correct that you will be stating your feelings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Can you please proceed, Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I start describing to you what happened in that unfortunate war, I would like to thank you for the understanding you have shown by cancelling our previous sentencing hearing, and that was due to the situation that I was experiencing at the time. I need to inform you that one of the reasons for the condition that I was in at the time was removed. I don't know how things are going to unfold in the future, but we will keep you informed. At any rate, I would like to thank you for your understanding. The proceedings today have been rather long, and since this involves some very serious matters that will determine my fate, you will understand that my concentration is not what it should be. Therefore, I would like to use my notes in order to address you so that I can speak from the heart. Your Honours, thank you for giving me the opportunity in this encounter with the truth to say a few words about myself and the war in which I took part, about the reasons for the war, tragic consequences, and my real role in the events which led me to appear before this Court. I was born in a country where, at the time when I was a child, when I attended school, an impression was created that all of the reasons that had until then caused small peoples living there to fight had ceased. I remember well my thoughts as a young man when I believed that I belonged to this fortunate generation which will never experience war and that all that was needed for a happy future was an honourable and proper attitude to work the society and work. Growing up with such beliefs and growing up in a poor family, while still a high school student, I received a scholarship which enabled me to continue my education. I enrolled into a very prestigious air force academy where I achieved great results in my studies. The profession that I required [as interpreted], that of a very sophisticated radar engineer, opened up great possibilities for me in life. In addition to that, a very brave, very decisive, young woman of a different faith and ethnic background but with similar convictions and values became my wife. We started a family without any prejudice. We were an example for all generations. At the time it seemed that nothing could be better or happier. However, different times came, times when people started splitting along religious or ethnic lines, times that did not allow one a lot of choice. The war broke out with lightning speed and forced me to accept the call given by my friends and neighbours to assist in the defence of our people. To remain with one's nation in difficult times was always considered an honourable choice. Although I had some different plans for myself, this unfortunate development of events determined my fate. The chance to leave that hell decreased on a daily basis and as did their demands to remain on their side, to stand by them. This is how I came to be a member of the worst war whichever took place in that area. The plans of great powers and ambitions of small nations to organise the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina in accordance with their wishes were not compatible. This conflict between great powers and small nations caused violence, and overnight animosity was created, as were alliances which were difficult to understand. Although I was not a political man, I had sufficient background in history in order to know that my Croatian nation which was not very numerous in Bosnia and Herzegovina had nevertheless very deep roots in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Due to the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, our people were exposed to great suffering, and I believe that it was my duty, my clear duty, to remain with my nation. Your Honours, this is my belief to this day. Since I was not active in politics nor did I participate in setting the goals of the war, I believed that the leadership was doing this wisely, the leadership that was entrusted with this. Unfortunately, the time and events which ensued showed that some of the decisions were neither wise nor responsible. The conflict between Croats and Muslims should not have happened. There are witnesses, and I have also provided some evidence to the Prosecution clearly showing that back in the summer of 1992 I took a decisive stand against mad action of Tihomir Blaskic and those who protected him and provoked this conflict in Central Bosnia. Due to my position, I was removed in early 1993 from all positions I held at the time, so that this man with the support of the same people could immediately after that start his second war against Muslims. Having a good reputation in both nations and risking my own life, I played a key role in stopping this completely senseless conflict which could not produce a winner. Your Honours, there are many witnesses who can testify about this, and there are numerous documents which I, through my cooperation, provided to the Prosecution. However, despite of everything, the same people basically deported me from Kiseljak which was my town. In late April of 1993, when visiting some relatives in Kiseljak, I found myself amid crucial events when the same people started their third war against Muslims. It was no longer possible to do anything that could have stopped this senseless plight of people, destruction of their homes and settlements. A scenario was set in motion, a scenario that I knew nothing about, neither did many people that I spoke to. However, based on what we could see, and based on what I could learn, it didn't take much to realise what was going on. There was no double chain of command, nor was there an interruption in communication between those issuing orders and what was going on. Everything unfolded precisely as Blaskic requested it, pursuant his decision or somebody's order. I hope that he will be forced to explain this. The second issue was conceived in the eyes of cowards when they had to avoid their own responsibility and catastrophic effects. Lack of knowledge of what was going on on the ground and due to distance and poor communication, all of these facts point to the direction of lack of sensible leadership. However, as was easy to predict, the fortunes of war changed direction and soon Croats were under an all-out attack. The situation -- the status of Croats living in Central Bosnia became a terrible one. They started making plans for moving out. I also provided evidence about this to the Prosecution. Then the same authors of war remembered me. Knowing that I previously held a high reputation among Muslims and their military commanders, they entrusted me with a role of a negotiator and later on appointed me commander who was tasked with saving whatever was there left to save. It was difficult to negotiate and convince the opposing side that something that wasn't true in fact was true. Fully aware of tragic consequences should the war continue, I did my best to put an end to this madness. Unannounced I went to the headquarters of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Visoko, and at the risk of being imprisoned, once again I attempted to negotiate the end of war. I did everything that they asked me to do, even what they themselves believed to be impossible. However, the spiral of violence had reached such a high level that it was impossible to even discuss a truce. The desire to survive is such that it is difficult to ensure that those who had suffered terrible personal losses will always act reasonably. How to act in compliance with what was permissible under the circumstances which themselves are so impermissible as that war was. Your Honours, I knew that a large number of people that were under my command had suffered a personal loss, a loss of their family members or homes. I knew that there were people with their human faults. However, it was impossible for me to predict how each of them was going to react under war circumstances. I carried out my tasks with the people I had under my command, not the people I wish I had under my command. I never ordered a crime to be committed. I only ordered the implementation of what was necessary in terms of our operations. Within the framework of my possibilities, I sanctioned certain acts straight away, some upon the advice of my associates and the authorities and institutions were recorded with the intention of taking the necessary steps and procedure at a time when this would not be counter-productive for the overall system of defence. I also stood up to lawlessness, very often at the risk of my own life, and this is borne out by the fact that the criminals from my own ethnic group attacked me very often and a number of times tried to abduct me and kill me. There are documents to bear that out and I have put them at the disposal of the Prosecution. I have said all this in order to paint a realistic picture of the situation and the circumstances I had to act in. My departure to Vares did not have as its aim to perpetrate any crime which would create as a response an attack by the BH army on Vares, after which the Croatian people would have to leave that territory. The attack launched by the BH army on Vares lasted for several days. It was already ongoing. The HVO Vares asked for assistance, and in following orders, the orders given to me by my superiors, I did everything in my power to do what I could to save the situation. Unfortunately, certain individuals and groups did not respect the instructions received from their superiors and in that very difficult and unforeseeable development of events a crime took place. Nonetheless, it should not have been a justification for the serious crimes which happened to the Croatian people later on in that same territory. Your Honours, from everything that I have said and that you have heard, I would like to say that I did not order that crime to take place nor did it take place with my knowledge but it did happen. It was affected by individuals and groups to which I was superior. So that is why I am held accountable. Just as a commander can bask in glory for his good acts, the acts that he accomplishes together with his soldiers, so also military ethics and honour make it incumbent upon him to accept responsibility for the evil deeds that were committed. I will accept your sentence and judgement bravely and courageously. I am very sorry for all the victims and suffering that took place in Stupni Do and Vares. Those victims were unnecessary, just as the war between two friendly nations was unnecessary. I should like to apologise to the families of the people who have suffered, expressing my full sympathies for having lost their -- and my regrets for the loss of their nearest and dearest. This comes from the heart, and it is my sincere regret, because I understand the pain and suffering. I know this because the war brought pain and suffering to my own family, as it did to many other families, regardless of their ethnicity. All those victims deserve the truth and justice, and my cooperation with the Prosecution is a contribution to the establishment of the truth and the acceptance of my responsibility of a man who is responsible but not broken, as my former attorney was prone to state. I am convinced that this grain of truth will be recognised and separated from the sea of lies which for years in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia have been put about -- about me by individuals and the intelligence services and media who are owned by various proprietors in order to make me keep quiet, to remain silent, and to cover up the truth, to cover up the truth about the policies and politics pursued, policies which have made my own people both victims and aggressors in their own country. Only the truth can help future generations, and I will tell the truth and defend the truth regardless of threats and physical assaults, indeed, which I experienced in the Detention Unit. Since those threats were not only held at me personally but at my entire family and, indeed, my Defence counsel as well, I should like to ask this Honourable Trial Chamber to use its influence to protect them. Those people who are afraid of the truth will stop at nothing and use subtle and dangerous methods which confirms the well-devised intelligence and media campaign launched in the Republic of Croatia against me after I had reached a plea agreement with the Prosecution. How else can one explain the writings of a very influential Croatian weekly which refers to Croatian intelligence services and the lies they put out that I was responsible for the terrible tragedy that took place at the Markale market in Sarajevo and as a threat to my family. If along with this monstrous lie they publish a photograph of my wife with my address and even the licence plates of our family car. Is that not a covered up invitation to the friends and family of those who suffered in that terrible crime to lynch my family in retaliation and revenge. And even more monstrous and worse lies were bandied about about me through a programme that is very popular on Croatia television immediately after the plea agreement was made and immediately after I recognised my guilt. I should like to mention that my former attorney took part in that television programme. I described him earlier on by just two words -- just two words. Such tricks that are being played and the fate of individuals in Croatia who cooperated with this Tribunal are a lesson for caution, that I should proceed with care and do everything to see that my family are safe. They are well tried and tested methods of the lackeys of the regime, of poodles and dogs from the intelligence service and security services, of former political clans and present-day political clans who were at the head of fateful events and who had our destiny in our hands in order to protect themselves. They are trying to cover up what actually happened and are doing their best to provide false evidence and proof and accuse others by doing so, and thus belittle this Tribunal before the eyes of the Croatian public as well. I know full well that the Prosecution is undertaking concrete steps to unmask certain false constructions that have been slipped into this Tribunal. And I sincerely hope that they will give me the opportunity of personally taking part in unmasking these untruths. Your Honours, I have done everything in my power to ensure that you arrive at the whole truth. Proof and evidence about everything that happened stand firmly, placed before you in your hands. I believe in your courage and your wisdom in weighing up a just sentence. I pray to God to give me the strength and health to persevere honourably and to go back to my family, which is blameless and who needs me very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: You may sit down, Mr. Rajic. Thank you very much for your statement, Mr. Rajic. I have -- like after your counsel's submission, I have an observation and one, perhaps, two questions. My observation is the same as my observation towards counsel -- the points counsel made or some of her points, and it is that also you in your statement have departed on a number of points from the facts as they were agreed in the plea agreement. So this Trial Chamber will only look at those facts and will base its sentencing judgement on those facts. Let me come to two questions. And if you wish, you can ask us to proceed to closed or to private session if you feel that the answer may -- that it may better -- that it be better for you to have the answer in closed session. My first question relates to your remorse, and I'm thinking of what counsel just said, that your remorse was first manifested on the moment of your arrest and that as from the very beginning you were willing to express your remorse. And so my question to you is: Why then did it take so long for you to plead guilty? Why haven't you given a sooner effect to that remorse? The second question relates to a question that I have already asked the Prosecutor and that is the possible connection to the procedure that was envisaged at a certain moment in time to send you back for trial to the courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which you opposed, if my understanding is correct. And your guilty plea came on a crucial moment in time in those months in 2005. Is there a link or is there no link? These are the two questions I would like you to answer, if you can. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the factual situation which was placed before you and signed by the Defence and by myself and by the Prosecution is the result of a compromise in a clash of arguments on both sides. What I am saying here today, I do not wish to challenge and contest the factual basis which was signed and which is the document that you have before you. I wanted to take advantage of this opportunity to talk about a broader context of events and my special role therein, and I do not think that there is anything bad in that. Since my case -- or rather, since I was a link in the chain, a military chain of command as it is linked to my superiors and the people before me, I wanted to briefly depict my role in everything that happened. So I wanted to show you what the situation was like, what life was like. Secondly, as far as my remorse is concerned, my remorse at this moment, at this point in time. I would like to tell you that I did not wish to escape the truth, not from the very first day. I informed my superiors realistically about everything that was going on. However, as you know, it was due to different interests that prevailed at that time and decided -- matters that were decided upon by much higher authorities. They asked me to behave in the way that I behaved. I had no choice in the matter. I was asked, and the Prosecution knows this full well and has received proof and evidence of that, that I was asked to behave in the manner in which I behaved. So it wasn't my own personal choice, either to be a fugitive, to hide, or to change my name. The second point is this: As soon as the indictment against me was raised, I asked - and there is written evidence about that - to be allowed to prepare my defence in order to appear before this Tribunal. I was told that they would help me -- that I would receive help, but that I should defend official policy that came from Zagreb. And there is evidence and proof of that as well. I showed these documents to the Prosecution. I was not able to agree to that. I was not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Do you wish to go into private session? No. Okay. Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, there's no need for us to go into private session. As I was saying, I did not agree to do that. I said that I would defend myself and nobody else, because I am the person accused. As to the other people who were accused, they could make their own choices and defend whom they desire. So faced with a situation of this kind, I was threatened. My preparation to come before this Tribunal was threatened. So they tried to manipulate me in order to open up the possibility for another accused, Mr. Blaskic specifically, should go through his legal proceedings for his trial to finish, because I -- they knew that I would not cover up the truth. I would not cover up the actual situation and truth about what had happened. They knew that, and they knew that this could be to the detriment of Mr. Blaskic, and that is why I entered into a system whereby I was manipulated. But once I came to realise that there were things going on behind the scenes in order to save certain individuals at the expense of others, I became active. I collected evidence and proof, and I was arrested at the point in time when I had no more interest in hiding in being a fugitive. So that's the truth of it. So my remorse has been present from day one, but they tried to manipulate me and I wasn't allowed to speak out and tell the truth because this would not have been in the interests of certain institutions or individuals. It would not have been to their advantage had I done so. And now can you repeat your third question, please, I've forgotten it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: The third question was whether there was a connection between your guilty plea and your wish not to be sent back to Bosnia and Herzegovina for a trial there, which was considered last year as from July by the Prosecution, which was put before the Referral Chamber. And then you entered your guilty plea, and after that the Prosecution decided to suspend the proceeding in attendance of the judgement on the sentencing. So my question is: Is there a linkage between the two, or is this just a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There is no coincidence and no link. There is no link. Because I expressed the desire to speak to the Prosecution as soon as I came to The Hague, but Attorney Olujic tried to obstruct that wish of mine. And before discussions started about my possible return to Sarajevo, I had a conversation with the Prosecution with the help of Mrs. Kosta. Those negotiations had been going on for quite some time and were almost nearing an end. All that remained to be done was to decide upon certain points with respect to the final version of the plea agreement, nothing more than that. So since the gentlemen of the Prosecution were brought in a situation from higher-up institutions to make a schedule of where people would be sent to complete their trials, they entered into a formal procedure without my knowledge. So from day one - and this can be borne out by Mr. Scott, I'm sure - from day one, I never linked the two events, I never made any connection between those two events. And I would like to appeal and call upon Mr. Scott to say that what I have been saying is indeed the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Rajic. Judge Nosworthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. You have said on more than one occasion during the course of your statement and in answer to questions that you were forced and ordered to commit the acts that you committed or you've pleaded guilty to, certainly, and to participate in the cover-up. Now, what would have been the consequences of your not committing the acts and not participating in the cover-up?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now it is going to be difficult to explain all of the motives which lead to these things happening. However, at the time as this was unfolding, as they started the game of cover-up, I was ordered and I was told that this was in the interest of higher aims. I was clearly told that they knew I was not responsible for what had happened. However, they had a different role for me in mind. They wanted me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I'm asking you what would have happened to you, essentially. What would the consequences have been had you not done what you were being requested to do. If you could try and answer that for me. I'm sorry to stop you, but please do go directly to what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have been removed from the HVO, disqualified, and this would have endangered my own life and that of my family. That was what the circumstances were at the time. Our fate would have been very questionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, my next question is that you spoke of having married somebody of a different ethnic group and religion. What ethnic group and religion was your wife, or is she?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fortunately she is still my wife and the mother of our three children, and we are expecting the fourth child. She hails from Macedonia. I married her while I served in the JNA in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My next question to you is that you had said that your chance to leave hell decreased. Were you referring to your participation in the war as hell, or what were you referring to? Could you just briefly tell us a little bit more about this hell?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My profession was not of a military nature. I had some other plans for myself because my education allowed me to find job in some other fields outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, as you know yourself, the entire Bosnia transformed into hell very quickly. All of the roads were very soon closed and obstructed and it was difficult to leave it, especially leave it with your entire family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that a number of the persons serving under you, under your command, had suffered personal losses as a result of the war. What about you, yourself? Had you suffered any personal losses or tragedies as a result of the war that you engaged in or -- please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My oldest brother lost his son, his only child, his only son. My younger brother became a disabled person. He has a 60 per cent disability. My other close relative lost his child, a minor at the time. In addition to that, in my more distant family there were other victims. So there is practically not a household within my whole family that has not suffered significant losses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to be very pointed when you're responding, and I want to find out from you, looking back at your childhood, did any traumatic incidents took place or anything happen during the course of your childhood, your formative years, your years as a young person before you became an adult, that could have impacted negatively on how you conducted yourself as an adult in later years and, more particularly, how you responded during the war in the command of the persons under you or in carrying out your duties as a man-of-war? Please be very pointed and get to the issue that I place before you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I come from a traditional and patriarchal and a very poor family. As for a specific event from my childhood, I do not remember one. As a boy, as a young man, and later as an officer and an adult I always received praise and commendation for all of my achievements, both at school and at work. A war is something that no prior life can prepare you for. No schooling can prepare you for war. I would like you to understand that. War puts you in a situation where you have to make split-second decisions, and you usually have to choose out of several evils. You normally never have to choose between good and evil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rajic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Judge Hoepfel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to have the picture complete, this one question. Although you were just saying no schooling can prepare you for war, I still would like to know about your education. Could you give us a short overview. It was mentioned that you attended secondary school. Where and how long and what other education did you enjoy?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completed secondary school for mechanical technicians in Sarajevo. I was an excellent student and I graduated with all straight A's. Following that, as a person holding military scholarship, I enrolled into air force academy department for computers. That was the most difficult specialty within the air force academy. I also graduated as top in my class. I was the best student in my class. I was an exemplary officer later on when I served in the JNA. My profession also allowed me to work as a flight controller in civilian aviation, which was my original plan had I succeeded in getting myself out of the hell of war which engulfed Bosnia and Herzegovina. My profession had nothing to do with the war. I wasn't a specialist needed in war. My profession is more of a civilian nature, that of an air flight controller. That was my occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are just on schedule. I think because we must close this session at 7.00. So according to our schedule, it is now for the Prosecution to make some closing remarks, five minutes maximum, and the same amount of time for the Defence. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try to move quite quickly in effect but hopefully not speak too fast for the translation. There are two cases in response to the question that the Judges -- Your Honours raised some time ago now about the aggravating factor. In the Celebici case, the appeal judgement, it's called the Delalic case but referenced often as the Celebici case, did in fact indicate that where an individual has been convicted of 7(1), the abuse of their role as a superior is, indeed, an aggravating factor. And more recently in the Stakic judgement of the 31st of July, 2003, in paragraph 9.12 indicates that, in fact -- and it says this: "If a conviction is entered under Article 7(1) only, the accused's position as a superior when proved beyond a reasonable doubt must be taken into account as an aggravating factor." So we bring those two items to the Court's attention. Also, quickly, I do -- I was able to locate and can provide to the Chamber after the hearing in the interests of time the copy of the document that Mr. Rajic signed on the 19th of January, 1996, indicating his knowledge of the charges in the pending indictment against him. I have that here. Also I have and I will give to the Registry a copy of the CD of the video that we played. So of course we will make that part of the record, and also I have a copy for each of the Judges, if you would like that. Very quickly, on the issue of the defenders in Stupni Do, let there be no mistake about that, the Prosecution position has never been that Stupni Do was a completely undefended village. And I believe we took pains in the factual basis to make sure, such as in paragraph 20, I believe, indicating exactly what the situation were. There were indeed defenders in the village, and I just -- forgive my artwork, but just to make the point. If this is the village and you put positions around the village facing outward, that is a defensive position. You're defending the village. If you surround a village and your positions are doing that, that is an offensive position. Stupni Do was defended. There were people there who did the best they could to keep these terrible things from happening, but unfortunately they couldn't stop it. Point number 2 -- we've never said that there were only six combatants in the village. What we have said was that we think -- we consider in our calculations that of the people killed, six might have been considered to be combatants, but not that there were only six combatants altogether, defenders, if you will, in the village. So to clarify that. Mr. Rajic has indicated that he, in fact, prosecuted people when misconduct came to his attention. Your Honours may recall that we have responded to that in our supplemental brief dated the 6th of March, 2006, and in the interests of time I will not repeat our arguments, but we provided the Chamber some additional documentation contrary to that allegation in our filing of the 6th of March, 2006. In connection with -- not perhaps a major point, but in connection with the bodies not even being proved to be individuals but perhaps were animals, all of these bodies, or at least those that could be recovered, were in fact autopsied by professionals after the investigation -- as a part of the investigation. They were identified as human remains. I'm afraid that as to some of what Mr. Rajic has said this afternoon about his involvement during the war, it's probably -- it's not that Mr. -- it's not the Ivica Rajic that was known to the Muslims in the Kiseljak region in 1993. And I would just in terms of time briefly refer the Chamber to the Kordic trial judgement which details the crimes committed throughout the Kiseljak region by Mr. Rajic's soldiers in June -- in particular in June of 1993. In terms of the mention about the cooperation that was made known to me or offered to me about the Blaskic case, Your Honours, all I can say is that there were times with Mr. Rajic's earlier counsel, previous counsel, there were long periods of complete non-communication. There were also times when certain information was offered to the Prosecution, if you will, on terms that were not acceptable to us. We simply said we were not interested in talking to them on that basis, and it was only until some many months later that, in fact, we have gotten to where we were. So I don't want there to be any misunderstanding about that. In terms of the 11 bis linkage, Mr. Rajic has asked me to confirm his account, and on that point I'm happy to say that, yes, our position on that is the same. There was no linkage except, as I said, we were on somewhat parallel tracks. So I will confirm and I think there's no disagreement on that. Let me conclude, Your Honours, with this final statement. As we said at the beginning, this Trial Chamber must impose a sentence upon the accused for the commission of crimes of the utmost gravity in which he as the commander was closely and substantially involved. The Tribunal must once again send the message that the Latin saying "in times of war the law falls silent" is no longer, if it ever was, international law, that criminals, even during war, indeed especially during war, must be held accountable. For all the reasons discussed, it still remains the Prosecution recommendation and our request to this Chamber and to your Honourable Judges that Mr. Rajic be sentenced to a total imprisonment of 15 years' imprisonment, taking into account about the aggravating and the mitigating factors. My final comment will be this, taking again from one of the victims. Quite ironic in a way when you hear these words, they seem quite gentle and quite soft in contrast to what happened on the 23rd of October. "At about 2.00 of the night" -- they mean 2.00 the next morning, in the middle of the night, on the morning of the -- 2.00 in the morning of the 24th -- "it was decided to leave the basement, so all of us left the basement. Outside it had stopped raining. The dark of the night was lightened by the flames that were eating the timber of our homes. The silence of the night would every now and then be broken by the crackle of the burning wood or the sound of ammunition going off on catching fire." How quickly that silence must have been replaced by crying. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. Ms. Kosta, five minutes. Do I take it that you don't want to make a closing -- okay. Thank you very much. Let me then turn to Mr. Rajic and ask him whether he has something to add. Ms. Kosta -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that I was still listening to the interpretation. I was listening to the interpretation, so I was unable to respond to your invitation. I would just like to say a few words, and then I would like to yield the floor to my client so that he can also address you. As the Prosecution stated that they provided valid evidence attempting to convince you that a 15-year sentence is fully appropriate, I also believe that within its ability the Defence provided all available documentation to assure you that an appropriate sentence in this case would be a 12-year sentence, in view of the status of my client at the time when the crime was committed and the consequences. I would also like for you to apply the principle of mens rea. I will now conclude my final address and say that the accused is faced himself -- and if this Trial Chamber does its job, then this sentence will be an exemplary sentence for the whole world. And I think that through his words and actions, my client has shown to you that it is human to err but it is divine to forgive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kosta. Mr. Rajic, do you want to add something at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, who participated in all of these events, am sometimes at a loss. It is difficult for me to explain the events which took place in my immediate vicinity. It is also hard in a short space of time to be convincing, even though I provided substantial evidence to Mr. Scott and the Prosecution about my conduct and my attitude towards Muslims, both in Kiseljak and elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as my attitude toward other ethnic groups. Once again, I regret that there were any victims in the war. I wish there had been no war and that I had not participated in that war, the war which took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that type of war. There is no military school that can prepare you for that type of war, and this is what I wanted to make clear in the courtroom. This is something that defies description, something that I will be unable to understand for the rest of my life. Thank you. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rajic, you may sit down. This brings this session to an end. The Trial Chamber will now adjourn and we will deliberate and give this judgement in due course. We can't say exactly when, but we will do it at the earliest possible moment. Thank you very much.
